Suppress quasi-identifiers until every subject reaches the target

Source: R/anon_suppress.R
anon_suppress.Rd

For subjects whose group is still smaller than the target after generalization, blanks quasi-identifier cells until every released pattern is shared by enough records (local suppression), or removes those subjects from every dataset. Risk is k-anonymity on the released table (see "After suppression" in anon_risk()): a blanked cell is a value of its own.

Usage

anon_suppress(
  data,
  quasi,
  key = "USUBJID",
  max_risk = 0.09,
  order = NULL,
  method = c("cells", "drop"),
  unresolved = c("drop", "keep"),
  key_cols = "RSUBJID",
  also = "SUBJID",
  everywhere = TRUE
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, a named list of data frames linked by key, or the result of an earlier step such as anon_generalize().

quasi

The quasi-identifiers to measure. For a single data frame, a character vector of column names. For a list of data frames, a list whose named elements are character vectors of columns in the dataset of that name (each subject must have one value per column, as in dm), and whose unnamed elements are anon_quasi_values() specifications for values that vary by row, such as baseline height and weight in vs.

key

Name of the subject identifier column shared by the datasets. It must have the same type (character or factor, or numeric) in every dataset used.

max_risk

Highest acceptable re-identification risk for any subject (the maximum risk, 1 / k for the smallest group). The target group size is the smallest k with 1 / k <= max_risk, allowing for floating-point error so that 0.1 and 1/3 give 10 and 3. The default, 0.09, is the threshold Health Canada and EMA encourage for public release of clinical information, and requires groups of at least 12. Health Canada equates 0.09 with a cell size of 11, but 1 / 11 is about 0.0909; to use groups of 11, pass max_risk = 1/11. See Details.

order

Names of quasi-identifiers (as anon_risk() names them) from least to most useful, to choose between blanking options that are otherwise equal: the most useful are blanked last. Those not listed follow, in the order of quasi. Default: the order of quasi, its first quasi-identifier being the first blanked.

method

"cells" (default) blanks cells; "drop" removes the subjects in groups smaller than the target from every dataset.

unresolved

With method = "cells", what to do with subjects still in groups smaller than the target when nothing is left to blank: "drop" (default) removes them from every dataset, with a warning; "keep" keeps them, with a warning.

key_cols

Names of columns holding other subjects' keys (default "RSUBJID", as in SDTM RELSUB): rows that refer to a removed subject are removed too, so no reference is left dangling.

also

Names of related identifier columns (default "SUBJID"): when subjects are removed, their values (of at least 5 characters, as anon_subject_ids() searches them) are looked for in what remains.

everywhere

Logical. If TRUE (default), a quasi-identifier given as a column (such as AGE in dm) is blanked for the subject in every dataset with the key that has a column of that name (such as AGE in an ADaM adsl or adae), and in data frames with the key nested in any dataset. If FALSE, only in its own dataset, and a warning names the other datasets that hold a column of that name.

Value

An object of class "anon_deid_step", as for anon_subject_ids(), with suppressed, the record of blanked cells (dataset, column or test, and subject key).

Details

The measure. Each released record's pattern is its visible quasi-identifier values plus the places of its blanked cells, a blanked cell counting as a value of its own; a subject's k is the number of released records with exactly its pattern, and every pattern must be shared by at least the target group size. Real missing values are values, distinct from blanked cells. Cells blanked by an earlier anon_suppress() in the same chain count as blanked. An attacker who knows a subject's values then finds at least k records that could be it, and records blanked everywhere only hide among each other.

Cells. The step repeats, on the records in groups smaller than the target: for each quasi-identifier still shown on some of them, it tries blanking that quasi-identifier on all of them. If a try brings records into groups of at least the target, it takes the try that brings the most (then needs the fewest cells, then blanks the least useful by order) and blanks only the records it brings in. Otherwise it takes the try that merges the most small patterns (then the least useful) and blanks it on all of them. Every step blanks at least one cell, so it ends. Then each group still too small (largest first; often the one blanked everywhere) is filled from donors: records of other groups that can spare them (their group keeps at least the target size), which take its pattern by blanking the cells where it is blank, the donors needing the fewest cells (then the least useful) first. Records still short (or with fewer subjects than the target group size) are unresolved. The result is deterministic and doesn't depend on the order of rows, but it isn't guaranteed to blank the fewest cells. Blanking only joins records into groups and removing small groups leaves the others as they are, so groups of at least the target stay so.

A quasi-identifier is blanked in every row of that subject: the column in every row of the subject in its dataset (and, with everywhere, in every other dataset with the key that has the column), and for an anon_quasi_values() specification every row of the test (not only the measured one), with its other results: for SDTM --ORRES, --STRESC and --STRESN; for ADaM AVAL, AVALC, BASE, BASEC, CHG, PCHG and R2BASE. Blanks are missing values: "" for text unless the column already uses NA for missing text (it has NA and no ""), NA for numbers and factors (a factor's levels held only by blanked values are dropped). Columns keep their type and attributes. The step records which cells it blanked (by subject key, as the data holds it, never values), and later steps carry the record on, so anon_risk() can measure the result.

Drop. Subjects in groups smaller than the target are removed (the other groups stay as they are). Removed subjects' rows go from every dataset with the key, from datasets whose rows belong to subjects through a packed column with the key or a list column of data frames holding one subject per row, from data frames with the key nested at any depth, and with the rows that refer to them in key_cols. If any removed subject's key, or a value of an also column, is still found in the text values of the data, a warning names the datasets.

The measure needs the step's record of blanked cells: measuring the data alone (a plain list of data frames) counts blanked cells as missing values, which can merge them with real missing values and call the target met when it isn't. Measure the step, as meets_target does.

When the target isn't met. settings$suppress$meets_target is FALSE, with reasons in settings$suppress$not_met, when the risk measured on the released data misses the target, when rows of removed subjects remain, when a copy of a column quasi-identifier in another dataset with the key shows a different value than its own dataset for a subject (for example AGE in adsl not generalized like AGE in dm), or when a dataset holding AGE as a quasi-identifier also holds a birth date more precise than a year (BRTHDTC, or a Date BRTHDT): with a reference date such as RFSTDTC, it gives the age back exactly, even after the dates were offset (both move together). Remove birth dates or reduce them to the year first. Other dates can give a quasi-identifier back the same way (an age at an event from --DTC, an ADaM AAGE), and so can derived columns (AGEGR1 from AGE, RACEN from RACE): list them as quasi-identifiers or generalize them together.

The log has one row per quasi-identifier (and result column) blanked, with the number of cells blanked and of subjects, one row per dataset with rows removed, and the risk before and after; it holds no values. The settings record the arguments and where each quasi-identifier comes from (not filter).

Each step of the loop groups the records once per quasi-identifier still shown on records short of the target; 10,000 subjects with 12 quasi-identifiers, all of them unique at first, take about a second.

See also

anon_risk(), anon_generalize()

Examples

dm <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = sprintf("S%02d", 1:6),
  AGE = c(30, 30, 30, 40, 40, 50),
  SEX = c("F", "F", "M", "M", "M", "F")
)
result <- anon_suppress(dm, quasi = c("AGE", "SEX"), max_risk = 1/2)
result$data
#>   USUBJID AGE SEX
#> 1     S01  30   F
#> 2     S02  30   F
#> 3     S03  NA    
#> 4     S04  40   M
#> 5     S05  40   M
#> 6     S06  NA    
anon_risk(result, quasi = c("AGE", "SEX"), max_risk = 1/2)
#> Re-identification risk
#> ======================
#> 
#> Quasi-identifiers: AGE, SEX 
#> Cells blanked by suppression: 4 (each a value of its own in the released pattern)
#> Subjects: 6 
#> Target: maximum risk 0.5 (groups of at least 2) 
#> Maximum risk: 0.5 (smallest group: 2)  Average risk: 0.5 
#> Unique subjects (group of 1): 0 
#> Subjects in groups smaller than 2: 0 (0%)
#> Meets target: yes 
#> 
#> Drivers (`_without` columns: result if that variable alone were left out):
#>  variable n_values n_missing n_unique_without n_below_k_without min_k_without
#>       AGE        2         2                0                 0             2
#>       SEX        2         2                0                 0             2
#>  avg_risk_without
#>               0.5
#>               0.5
